problem: The lead says t is 'a standard normal divided by a scaled chi-square'. The denominator is the square root of a scaled chi-square, not the scaled chi-square itself, so the one-line summary is slightly wrong even though the formula later in Section 2 is correct.
fix: Say: t is a standard normal divided by the square root of a scaled chi-square.

problem: S² is called 'sample variance' but its divisor is not fixed. The statement (n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1) is only true when S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n−1); if a student uses the divisor-n version, the formula fails.
fix: Define S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n−1), the sample variance with divisor n−1, and state that (n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1) for a normal population.

where: Section 2, sentence on when t is used
problem: 'We use t when σ is unknown and the sample is small' suggests t is only valid for small samples. The definition given just above holds for any sample size n from a normal population; small n is only a rule of thumb for when the difference from z matters.
fix: Say: when σ is unknown we use t for any n if the population is normal; the difference from z is large only for small n.

problem: The figure names the denominator chi-square of F as W and the numerator as U, while Section 3 writes the same two variables as U and V. V is already used for the chi-square inside t in Section 2, so students may connect the wrong nodes to the F formula.
fix: Use one set of names throughout, e.g. U and W for the two chi-squares in F, or add a note in Section 3 that V in the formula plays the role of W in the figure.
